A1.justification: This 'model' is fundamentally unacceptable. The insistence on *any* predictive element, even with severely restricted data use, prioritizes quantification over ethical considerations and student agency. Despite the workshop’s focus on nuanced discussion, this specification still attempts to categorize students as ‘at-risk’, which feels deeply problematic. The limited gains in identification do not justify these risks. We should invest solely in universally accessible support systems, not surveillance-based interventions.

A2.justification: This ‘model’ is deeply problematic. The conditions for data use are so restrictive as to render it almost useless, while the acceptance of a fairness trade-off – sacrificing 5 students per 100 – feels ethically unacceptable. The limited explainability threshold also raises concerns; even moderate opacity undermines trust. Ultimately, this specification reflects an attempt to compromise on fundamentally flawed premise - predicting student difficulties is not the right approach. I would block implementation and advocate for investment in universal support systems instead.

A3.justification: This 'provisional' specification is fundamentally unacceptable. Ultimately, this 'model' prioritizes avoiding risk over actually supporting those who need it and reinforces my conviction that we should focus on systemic improvements rather than predictive technology.
